claims.text: Enhanced chemical short-range order in FCC high-entropy alloys increases local bonding strength.
Enhanced chemical short-range order impedes dislocation motion.
Enhanced chemical short-range order elevates yield strength relative to a random atomic distribution.
Chemical short-range order alters deformation and work-hardening behavior.
CoCrFeMnNi is an FCC high-entropy alloy suitable for the proposed comparison.
An as-cast or solution-treated CoCrFeMnNi alloy can have minimal pre-existing short-range order.
Prolonged annealing promotes the development of chemical short-range order.
Rapid water quenching preserves a predominantly random solid solution with low short-range order.
The degree and spatial extent of chemical short-range order can be characterized using atom probe tomography and high-resolution TEM.
Localized regions of enhanced bonding produced by short-range order obstruct dislocation nucleation and propagation.
An annealed, short-range-order-enriched alloy will have higher yield strength than a rapidly quenched alloy.
An annealed, short-range-order-enriched alloy will exhibit altered work-hardening behavior and may have reduced ductility.
The proposed short-range-order effect should hold in FCC high-entropy alloys such as CoCrFeMnNi during quasi-static deformation at room temperature and approximately 400 degrees Celsius.
Significant secondary-phase formation or grain growth may invalidate the proposed relationship between short-range order and mechanical behavior.
Precisely isolating short-range order from other microstructural variables is challenging.
The degree and extent of short-range order depend on processing or loading conditions and can be associated with variation in mechanical response.
Samples with the same nominal composition, grain size, and phase constitution but different measured short-range order provide the intended controlled comparison.

Failure to observe a statistically significant yield-strength increase, a work-hardening change, or a correlation between short-range-order metrics and mechanical performance would falsify the hypothesis.
